analysis.one_liner: Delays major federal regulations until every court challenge against them is finished.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never advanced past its committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped any new federal rule expected to cost the economy $1 billion or more a year from taking effect until every lawsuit against it was fully resolved. Before a rule could even be finalized, the agency would have to send it to a White Budget office to be labeled "high-impact." The practical effect is that a single lawsuit could keep a major new rule — on pollution, worker safety, or financial abuse — frozen for years while courts decide the case. The bill was introduced by one senator, attracted no cosponsors, and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and trade groups that would be subject to major new regulations. Under the bill, any regulated party could file a lawsuit and automatically freeze a $1-billion-a-year rule for the entire length of the court case — often years — even if the challenge was weak and eventually lost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated companies facing major new rules

how_it_helps.text: A final rule could not be published or take effect until the agency submitted it to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs and that office determined whether it is a "high-impact rule" that may impose an annual cost on the economy of at least $1 billion.
Once a rule is labeled high-impact, the agency must postpone its effective date until the final disposition of all lawsuits seeking judicial review of the rule.

If no one files a lawsuit within the review window — 60 days if the underlying statute sets none — the rule can take effect when that period ends, so the freeze applies only when a challenge is actually filed.
The bill also states that nothing in it limits courts from issuing their own orders blocking a rule, which would leave existing judicial delay tools in place alongside the new automatic freeze.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who the delayed rules were written to protect — workers, consumers, and communities waiting on major new health, safety, environmental, or financial protections — plus the agencies whose rulemaking gets bottlenecked through an extra review step.
analysis.who_pays_short: People waiting on new health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: A single lawsuit — even a weak one that ultimately fails — would automatically freeze a high-impact rule until all court review is finished, and major-rule litigation routinely takes years, so protected groups could wait out the delay with no showing that the rule is actually flawed.
The extra requirement that every final rule be sent to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for a cost determination adds a review step to rulemaking before rules can even be published.

A supporter's best-faith argument is that courts today can leave questionable rules in effect while cases drag on, causing harm during that time; the bill answers that by flipping the default so the rule waits instead. The cost of that default falls on the people the rule was meant to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers regulated companies a powerful tool: sue, and the rule freezes for years. It gives people waiting on protections nothing except a promise that the rule takes effect if nobody sues. Because $1 billion is an economy-wide cost figure that many major health, safety, and environmental rules would meet, the delay mechanism would apply broadly, and the burden of delay falls on the public rather than on the parties challenging the rule.

outcome.mechanism: One senator introduced it, it was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, no cosponsors ever signed on, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dan Sullivan introduced the bill on April 20, 2021.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; the action history shows no further action of any kind.

The bill would have barred any final rule from taking effect until a White House regulatory office determined whether it is a high-impact rule, defined as one that may cost the economy at least $1 billion a year.
High-impact rules would have had their effective dates postponed until every lawsuit seeking judicial review of the rule was finally resolved.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without a committee markup or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the default stayed in place: major new regulations can take effect while court challenges play out, so workers, consumers, and communities waiting on new protections are no worse off, and regulated industries did not get an automatic freeze tool.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People waiting on new regulations; the freeze tool never arrived

against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 20, 2021 and never held a markup, reported the bill, or moved it forward; it died in committee.

against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate and its committee agenda
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor or advance it through committee during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor attracted zero cosponsors from either party, and the bill went no further in a Senate run by Democrats [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Heavily regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: Any rule expected to cost the economy $1 billion or more a year could be frozen for years by one lawsuit, which would delay health, safety, environmental, and financial protections those companies would otherwise have to follow. The cost of delay falls on the people the rules protect.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and the regulatory system
industries.note: Agencies would face an extra mandatory review step before publishing any final rule, and their rules would sit unenforced during litigation. The public loses protection during those delays.
